reference.source: Renal tubulopathy and clinical genetics references
clinicalPearls: Caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in NR3C2, the gene encoding the mineralocorticoid receptor, producing renal resistance to aldosterone.
A renal-limited (target-organ) disorder characterised by salt wasting, hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis with markedly elevated renin and aldosterone.
Distinguished from the autosomal recessive systemic form, which is caused by epithelial sodium channel subunit genes (SCNN1A, SCNN1B, SCNN1G) and is more severe and multisystem.
Presents in the neonatal period with poor feeding, vomiting, dehydration, salt craving and failure to thrive.
Symptoms typically improve with age, so salt supplementation can often be reduced or withdrawn in later childhood.
Aldosterone is high because of receptor resistance, which separates it from adrenal insufficiency and aldosterone synthesis defects where aldosterone is low.
Blood pressure is normal or low, in contrast to pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2 (Gordon syndrome), which causes hypertension with hyperkalaemia.
Sweat, salivary and colonic electrolyte handling are normal, unlike in the recessive systemic form.
reference.pathophysiology: Autosomal dominant pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in NR3C2, the gene encoding the mineralocorticoid receptor. Aldosterone normally acts through this receptor in the principal cells of the distal nephron to promote sodium reabsorption through the epithelial sodium channel while facilitating potassium and hydrogen ion excretion. Receptor haploinsufficiency renders the distal tubule resistant to aldosterone, so despite intense stimulation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis the kidney cannot conserve sodium, resulting in renal salt wasting, hyperkalaemia and a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis with strikingly elevated plasma renin and aldosterone. Because the defect is confined to the mineralocorticoid receptor, disease is renal-limited and other aldosterone target tissues such as the sweat glands, salivary glands and colon behave normally, in contrast to the multisystem autosomal recessive form caused by defects in the epithelial sodium channel subunits. Residual receptor function and maturation of distal sodium handling with age account for the characteristic clinical improvement during childhood.
additionalDifferentials: Autosomal recessive pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 (SCNN1A, SCNN1B, SCNN1G / epithelial sodium channel) — severe, systemic and persistent
Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2 / Gordon syndrome (WNK1, WNK4, KLHL3, CUL3) — hyperkalaemia with hypertension and metabolic acidosis
Primary adrenal insufficiency or adrenal hypoplasia — salt wasting with low aldosterone
Salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency) — with abnormal 17-hydroxyprogesterone
Aldosterone synthase deficiency (CYP11B2) — salt wasting with low aldosterone
Secondary or transient pseudohypoaldosteronism from urinary tract infection or obstructive uropathy
Type 4 (hyperkalaemic) renal tubular acidosis from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Serum electrolytes and venous blood gas showing hyperkalaemia, hyponatraemia and metabolic acidosis
Plasma renin activity and aldosterone, both characteristically and markedly elevated
Serum cortisol and 17-hydroxyprogesterone to exclude adrenal insufficiency and congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Spot urinary sodium and potassium demonstrating inappropriate natriuresis for the clinical state
Renal tract ultrasound and urine culture to exclude secondary or transient pseudohypoaldosteronism from obstruction or infection
Molecular genetic testing of NR3C2, with epithelial sodium channel subunit genes considered if systemic features are present
Sweat test where the systemic recessive form is being considered
redFlags: Severe hyperkalaemia with electrocardiographic changes or cardiac arrhythmia
Hyponatraemic hypovolaemic shock in the neonate
Failure to thrive with recurrent salt-wasting crises
Misattribution to an adrenal crisis leading to inappropriate mineralocorticoid therapy
reference.prognosis: The renal-limited autosomal dominant form typically improves through infancy and childhood, so that salt supplementation can often eventually be reduced or withdrawn, and the long-term prognosis is good. This contrasts sharply with the persistent, multisystem autosomal recessive form.
pitfalls: Diagnosing adrenal insufficiency despite the high, rather than low, aldosterone
Missing secondary or transient pseudohypoaldosteronism caused by urinary tract infection or obstructive uropathy
Confusing the renal-limited autosomal dominant form with the severe systemic autosomal recessive form
Weaning salt supplementation too early and precipitating a salt-wasting crisis
